extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a claimed invention satisfies the statutory utility requirement (35 U.S.C. §101) and related considerations under 35 U.S.C. §112 (first paragraph), including what counts as specific, substantial, and credible utility in patent examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of situations not defining "substantial utilities"
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are examples of situations that require or constitute carrying out further research to identify or reasonably confirm a 'real world' context of use and, therefore, do not define 'substantial utilities': (A) Basic research such as studying the properties of the claimed product itself or the mechanisms in which the material is involved; (B) A method of treating an unspecified disease or condition; (C) A method of assaying for or identifying a material that itself has no specific and/or substantial utility; (D) A method of making a material that itself has no specific, substantial, and credible utility; and (E) A claim to an intermediate product for use in making a final product that has no specific, substantial and credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These situations are examples where further research is required and do not by themselves establish a substantial utility. Office personnel should treat such assertions as requiring additional support before accepting utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'immediate benefit to the public'
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must be careful not to interpret the phrase 'immediate benefit to the public' to mean that products or services based on the claimed invention must be 'currently available' to the public in order to satisfy the utility requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any reasonable use identified by the applicant that can be viewed as providing a public benefit should be accepted as sufficient, at least with regard to defining a 'substantial' utility (citing Brenner v. Manson). Examiners should not require commercial availability or FDA approval as a condition of patent utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research tools and 'research use' labels are not dispositive of lack of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels such as 'research tool,' 'intermediate' or 'for research purposes' are not helpful in determining if an applicant has identified a specific and substantial utility for the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many research tools (e.g., gas chromatographs, screening assays, nucleotide sequencing techniques) have clear, specific and unquestionable utility. Examination must distinguish inventions that have a specifically identified substantial utility from those whose asserted utility requires further research to identify or reasonably confirm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative inventions and 'incredible' utility threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that is 'inoperative' (i.e., it does not operate to produce the results claimed) is not 'useful' under the patent law, but to violate 35 U.S.C. 101 the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small degree of utility is sufficient; partial success is enough. Rejections as inoperative are rare and should be based on clear evidence of total incapacity. Do not label an asserted utility 'incredible' or 'speculative' unless the record supports that a rejection for lack of utility is proper. Examples of truly inoperative claims (perpetual motion, cold fusion, etc.) are fact-specific and not a per se rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic or pharmacological utility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions asserted to have utility in the treatment of human or animal disorders are subject to the same legal requirements for utility as inventions in any other field of technology; identification of a pharmacological activity relevant to an asserted use provides an 'immediate benefit to the public' and thus satisfies the utility requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of pharmacological activity (including in vitro testing) can establish practical utility (Nelson v. Bowler, Cross v. Iizuka). FDA approval or clinical phase testing is not required to satisfy patent utility; the stage at which utility exists is well before human administration. Examiners should rely on case law (Nelson, Jolles, Cross, Brana) when evaluating such assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deficiency under the utility prong of 35 U.S.C. 101 also creates a deficiency under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; 35 U.S.C. 112 presupposes compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection properly imposed under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility should be accompanied by a separate 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection that incorporates the factual basis and conclusions from the 101 rejection. Conversely, do not impose a 112 first paragraph rejection on 'lack of utility' grounds unless a proper 101 rejection exists. Note that 112 also addresses matters distinct from utility (support, enablement, written description, best mode). Rejections grounded on non-utility 112 issues should be stated separately from 101 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-focused evaluation and genus/species treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention (each claim) is the focus of the utility requirement; each claim must be evaluated on its own merits. Generally a dependent claim will have utility if the independent claim to which it refers defines an invention having utility. Where an applicant has established utility for a species within a genus, a generic claim to the genus should generally be treated as sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 101 unless it can be established that other species encompassed by the claim lack utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If certain species clearly lack utility, encourage amendment of the generic claim to exclude those species. Ensure that when a dependent claim specifies a different utility than the independent claim, that difference is evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: One credible assertion of specific utility suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not credible, do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a properly claimed invention meets at least one stated objective, utility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is shown. Case citations: Raytheon v. Roper, In re Gottlieb, In re Malachowski.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and substantial utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant believes the invention is useful; it must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the applicant believes the claimed invention is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized assertions (e.g., 'biological activity', 'biological properties', 'plastic-like') without explanation of why that activity is useful are insufficient (citing Brenner v. Manson; In re Kirk; In re Ziegler). A disclosure that identifies a particular biological activity and explains how that activity can be utilized in a therapeutic application does contain an assertion of specific and substantial utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-established utility exception
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has a well-established utility if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on its characteristics, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention has well-established utility, rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, should not be imposed. Example: cloning the sequence of a well-known protein such as insulin where the use of insulin is well known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when no statement of utility appears in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If no statements asserting a specific and substantial utility are found in the specification, Office personnel should determine if the claimed invention has a well-established utility; if not, the examiner should reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should clearly indicate failure to identify a specific and substantial utility and require the applicant to reply indicating why the invention is believed useful and where support for the asserted utility can be found in the specification as filed. See MPEP §2701 for further procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of utility created by applicant's assertion and initial examiner approach
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's assertion of utility creates a presumption of utility that will be sufficient in most cases to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101; examiners must begin by asking if there is any reason to question the truth of the statement of utility rather than assuming it false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Langer test: a disclosure teaching making/using the invention in terms corresponding in scope to the claim must be taken as in compliance with enablement unless there is reason to doubt the objective truth of statements relied upon. Examiners should evaluate the logic and any evidence provided by the applicant before challenging utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard to overcome presumption of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome the presumption of utility, Office personnel must establish that it is more likely than not that a person of ordinary skill in the art would doubt the truth of the applicant's statement of utility; the evidentiary standard is a preponderance of the totality of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide facts and reasoning sufficient to show a person of ordinary skill would consider the asserted utility false. After applicant reply, patentability is determined on the totality of the record considering persuasiveness of argument (citing In re Oetiker, Corkill, Herman v. Huddleston). Evidence presented by examiner must counter applicant's supporting facts/reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an asserted utility is not credible
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertion of utility is not credible if (A) the logic underlying the assertion is seriously flawed, or (B) the facts upon which the assertion is based are inconsistent with the logic underlying the assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility is assessed by the reliability of the statement based on the logic and facts offered. Office personnel cannot merely dismiss a specific asserted utility as 'wrong' without demonstrating that one of these criteria is met; must present why a person of ordinary skill would not believe the assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limits on examiner reliance on applicant's prosecution statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or incident to prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office should not require an applicant to strike nonessential statements relating to utility from a disclosure if technical accuracy cannot be easily confirmed and those statements are not necessary to support patentability. Examiners should avoid reading unclaimed limitations or unclaimed embodiments into claims when evaluating utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph) addresses more than utility
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, addresses whether claims are fully supported by the disclosure, whether the disclosure is enabling, and whether the written description and best mode requirements are satisfied — matters separate from the question of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclosure showing a specific and credible utility and credible basis does not necessarily satisfy all 112 requirements. For example, an invention may have utility but the specification may not enable one of ordinary skill to practice the full scope of claimed subject matter, in which case a 112 rejection (not based on utility) may be appropriate and should be imposed separately from utility-based rejections.
